title: Turnkey Recovery Amenity Operator for Landlords
one_liner: Operate managed sauna-and-cold-plunge suites inside apartment and mixed-use buildings, paid a flat monthly fee by the landlord.
customer: Owners and operators of multifamily, mixed-use and office buildings with underused fitness rooms and an amenity-arms-race problem.
problem: Insiders treat recovery as a consumer studio business (one brand went from zero to 25 contrast-therapy studios in about 20 months and plans 100 more), with retail rent, foot-traffic marketing and wet/hot-room liability. Meanwhile landlords already own the square footage and want differentiators, but cannot operate saunas and plunge tubs (cleaning, water treatment, safety, insurance).
solution: Design, install (modular saunas and tubs) and operate a recovery suite: booking app, resident access control, daily cleaning and water testing, camera-free safety monitoring, waiver and insurance management. The landlord pays a flat monthly operating fee; residents can pay small fees for guests or premium hours.
why_now: Nordic-style social wellness attendance grew about 33 percent in 2025, sauna and cold-plunge hardware is a $1B+ market and getting cheaper, and HSA-linked home sauna sales show pre-tax demand exists even without a studio.
revenue_model: $3-8k per month per property operating fee (or revenue share above a threshold) plus $40-120k build-out margin.
non_obvious_insight: The best customer for the sauna boom is not the Gen Z consumer but the landlord: acquisition cost is one sales call instead of a marketing budget, and what the landlord is really buying is zero-liability operation, not wellness.
first_30_days: Cold-outreach 100 mid-size multifamily owners in one metro with underused amenity rooms, then pilot one building with a rented modular sauna and a $3k plunge tub on a 90-day contract at about $2.5k per month while tracking resident usage and renewal intent.

title: Model-of-Origin Forensics for AI Music Catalogs
one_liner: Attribute a track to the generator and version that made it, so catalog owners and litigators can separate legacy unlicensed-model output from the rest.
customer: Distributors, sync and production-music libraries, entertainment law firms and insurers, plus brand legal teams clearing ad music.
problem: Suno replaced its models on Sep 9 with one trained on licensed music, after label suits. A second UMG/Sony suit over roughly 60k songs is reported (single source, verify). Warner settled. Tens of millions of tracks from older models are already distributed or embedded in videos and ads. Downstream legal exposure is unproven, but risk-averse counsel will want to know which tracks came from which model. Deezer's detector answers 'AI or not,' and is licensed only to platforms.
solution: A classifier and evidence report attributing audio to a generator family and version range (Suno, Udio, Stable Audio, ElevenLabs Music and others), trained on labeled corpora we generate ourselves from paid subscriptions to each version. Output: family, version range, confidence, and whether a post-Aug 6 Suno watermark is present. Includes catalog-level exposure heat maps, a batch API, and expert-witness-ready reports.
why_now: Suno's Sep 9 model swap and Aug 6 watermarking pledge create a hard before-and-after line. Pre-watermark, pre-swap tracks are exactly the legacy tail that needs forensic attribution, and the lawsuits make the question urgent.
revenue_model: $0.05-0.25 per track for batch screening, $5-50k per catalog audit, $15-75k per litigation-grade report, and annual retainers for law firms and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is building 'AI or not' detectors, which are crowded and sell at consumer prices ($20/month). Nobody sells 'which model, which version, before or after the licensed swap.' That is the question that maps to legal liability, so it prices like legal risk.
first_30_days: Subscribe to the major generators and produce about 5k labeled tracks per version. Get a baseline classifier working in three weeks. Approach five sync libraries and two boutique entertainment-law firms, and sell $10k pilot audits of a 20k-track catalog subset.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.

title: Microschool Compliance Kit With Built-In Insurance
one_liner: State-by-state registration, safeguarding, ESA and scholarship vendor onboarding, records and liability insurance sold as one subscription to microschool founders.
customer: Microschool founders and learning-pod operators (10-40 students each) and microschool networks; about 1,000 microschools are reportedly in limbo awaiting federal tax-credit rules.
problem: Microschool legal status differs by state, scholarship-credit eligibility rules are unresolved, ESA vendor marketplaces are closed and painful to enter, and insurers are wary of unregulated child programs. Founders are ex-teachers and parents drowning in paperwork, and states are scrutinizing (Pennsylvania cited Alpha School for significant deficiencies).
solution: A compliance operating system: a state legal-status wizard, prefilled filings, fire and occupancy checklists, background-check and mandated-reporter workflows, attendance and records, ESA vendor applications and invoicing, and a bundled liability and abuse-and-molestation policy through an MGA partnership.
why_now: The scholarship credit begins in 2027 in 31 states, ESA programs are expanding (Texas had 200k+ applicants), and the microschool count is growing while final rules are in flux.
revenue_model: $199-399 per month per school SaaS, insurance commission of 15-20% on premiums of about $2-6k per school-year, and a $500 ESA vendor concierge fee.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is not software but insurability. Insurers will price a standardized, audited operating model far better than a random pod, and whoever accumulates loss-ratio data first sets the industry standard.
first_30_days: Pick two ESA states, build checklists and a $750 'launch audit', and sell to 20 founders through microschool founder groups. Pre-negotiate terms with an MGA or broker.

title: Battery EPR Desk for E-Mobility Importers
one_liner: A retainer compliance service that registers, reports and budgets for battery EPR on behalf of small e-bike, scooter and power-station brands.
customer: E-bike, e-scooter, power-station and power-tool brand owners and importers of record selling into California and other battery-EPR states, typically $2-100M revenue with no regulatory staff.
problem: California signed SB 501 on Sept 20, 2026, creating medium-format battery EPR with a 60% recycling-efficiency floor. Thousands of small importers and marketplace sellers cannot parse who counts as the producer, how to pick or join a PRO, or what to report. Their packs also drive facility fires.
solution: Producer determination, PRO registration, automated unit and weight reporting from Shopify and Amazon data, fee budgeting, labeling artwork, take-back partnering, and a battery data sheet (chemistry, mass, removability). Recyclers want that sheet, and the evidence pack satisfies audits.
why_now: SB 501 was signed days ago, and California signed it while vetoing other bills. Existing state battery laws and the 74 catastrophic facility fires this year mean regulators and marketplaces will demand proof.
revenue_model: $6-24K per year retainer, plus 5-10% markup on pass-through PRO fees and take-back costs.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the famous brand but 3,000 small importers who cannot read statute. Becoming the compliance layer that marketplaces reference flips the distribution problem.
first_30_days: Build an 'Am I a producer?' quiz. Scrape marketplaces for e-mobility brands selling into California and email 300. Sign 10 for a $1.5K registration audit. Approach one marketplace's compliance team.

title: Cash Caregiver Rails: Deductible, Reimbursable, Legal
one_liner: Payroll plus clinician plan-of-care paperwork that turns cash-paid family and neighbor caregivers into tax-deductible, insurance-reimbursable, workers'-comp-covered employment.
customer: Adult children and spouses who pay $15-30 an hour in cash to informal home aides for a parent with dementia, frailty or serious illness. The households spend $20-60K a year, and some have long-term care insurance.
problem: A large slice of elder home care runs on cash, word of mouth and no paperwork. Families lose tax deductions and long-term care insurance benefits that require documentation. They carry unlimited liability for injuries in their home and owe unpaid household-employer taxes. The aide has no wage record, comp cover, or path to benefits. Agencies solve this at $35+ an hour, which many families can't afford.
solution: An employer-of-record service for family-hired caregivers. It provides payroll, tax filing (household employer) and workers' comp or injury cover. A telehealth nurse practitioner certifies chronic illness and writes a plan of care, which are the tax and long-term care insurance requirements for 'qualified long-term care services'. A claims-ready packet is generated for long-term care insurers and the family's tax preparer, and a shift-check-in log is kept. Optional backup-aide pool for absences.
why_now: Boomers are in their 80s. Agency costs keep rising, and 2025-26 Medicaid funding cuts push more families toward informal care. Telehealth nurse practitioner visits make chronic-illness certification cheap. Household payroll rails and workers'-comp programs for single-worker households are now easy to embed through APIs.
revenue_model: $99-149 per household per month platform fee plus payroll processing. An annual $150-250 clinician certification fee. An insurer-paid fee, or employer benefit contract, for claim-ready documentation that reduces fraud and denial disputes. Backup-aide shifts at a margin.
non_obvious_insight: Families don't pay for compliance. They pay when the paperwork unlocks money that is currently being left on the table: deductions and insurance benefits that are only available to a documented, plan-of-care relationship. The clinician certification is the wedge, and payroll is just plumbing. Selling it as 'get reimbursed' rather than 'stay legal' changes conversion completely. It also builds a data asset that insurers will pay for.
first_30_days: Partner with a tax-preparer network or elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers who see cash caregivers daily. Contract a telehealth nurse practitioner group for plan-of-care certifications. Use an existing household payroll provider under white-label. Sign 15 families at $99/month with a money-back guarantee tied to documented reimbursements. Measure recovered dollars per household as the headline metric.

title: Human Concierge for Phone-Free Adults
one_liner: A $29 per month phone number staffed by humans who handle the app-only chores of modern life (QR menus, parking, rides, boarding passes, 2FA migration) so people can keep their dumbphone.
customer: Adults 25-55 who switched to flip phones, a Light Phone or a stripped-down iPhone, or want to but keep failing; first found in dumbphone communities and among buyers of minimalist phone brands, then tech workers and parents who go phone-free alongside their teens.
problem: People do not abandon dumbphones from lack of willpower but from friction: authenticator-only two-factor logins, QR-code menus, parking and transit apps, rideshare, mobile boarding passes and app-only bank features. Then they buy the smartphone back. Device makers respond by adding features (cameras, maps, apps), which recreates the problem. As the flip-phone revival hits the mainstream in 2026, the failure rate is the business opportunity.
solution: Two products. First, a one-time 'Switch Day' ($99): a human sits with the customer for two hours, ports the number, migrates 2FA away from authenticator apps to hardware keys, voice codes or email, moves bank alerts to text and voice, prints backup codes and paper maps. Second, 'the Desk', a call/text line staffed by humans with a company smartphone and virtual cards: they book the ride to your address, pay the parking zone by plate, read you the QR menu, print or hand over the boarding pass, and make the reservation that only exists in an app. Fair-use unlimited requests on the subscription, with pay-per-errand for heavier tasks.
why_now: The dumbphone and analog movement hit mainstream press in 2026 (Fortune's Gen Z analog coverage in February, new flip-phone startups launching in September), while schools in about 40 states now restrict phones, pushing parents to model the behavior. Meanwhile, essential services keep going app-only. Cheap voice and workflow tools let a small human team serve dozens of subscribers per agent.
revenue_model: $29 per month subscription, $99 Switch Day setup fee, bundle and referral deals with dumbphone makers (a Desk membership included with each device), employer perk for 'focus' or wellness programs, and per-errand fees for premium requests.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce product in the anti-screen economy is not another device but human proxies for the smartphone-shaped holes in society. The business grows every time a restaurant or city makes something QR-only, and every new mandate is a marketing lead. Abstainers are also a tight, vocal community, so each retained customer is an ambassador, and the manufacturers gain from a service that reduces returns.
first_30_days: Offer 20 people in dumbphone communities a free Switch Day in exchange for interviews and permission to log every request. Run the Desk by hand from one shared iPhone, a Google Voice number and an Airtable. Categorize the first 300 requests to find the top 10 that drive 80% of the pain. Convert users to $29 per month and approach two minimalist phone brands about bundling. Target 100 paying members by month 5.

title: Elder-Intelligible Voice for Healthcare AI Calls
one_liner: An audio layer that reshapes AI-agent voices so listeners 75+ with age-related hearing loss actually understand phone calls, sold per minute to healthcare voice-agent companies.
customer: Healthcare voice-AI vendors, pharmacies, payers and IVR providers whose outbound calls mostly reach people over 70.
problem: Voice agents are being deployed to call seniors about refills, discharge follow-ups and plan outreach. TTS is tuned for young ears, and phone audio cuts off above roughly 3.4 kHz, which is exactly where age-related hearing loss erases consonants (s, f, th, sh). Seniors mishear dates and doses, get frustrated and hang up. The vendor logs it as 'low engagement' and blames the patient.
solution: A drop-in post-processor between the TTS engine and the telephony stream: clear-speech prosody (slower on key phrases, pauses, sharper consonant timing), spectral reshaping tuned to typical presbycusis profiles, and optional per-caller calibration ('say the number you hear'). Add built-in comprehension checks like read-back of the dose. Prove it with a benchmark from a paid panel of 100 older listeners that shows word-recognition gains, then ship it as an API billed per audio minute.
why_now: Healthcare voice agents scaled fast in 2025-26 and their audience is old. Research already shows a clear-speech intelligibility benefit for synthetic voices. Low-latency neural audio processing is now cheap, and no one yet owns the psychoacoustics layer that sits under all those voices.
revenue_model: $0.01-0.03 per audio minute as an add-on, with enterprise minimums of $2-5k/month. Paid listening-panel certification packages (~$15k) that customers can cite in compliance and sales.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats 'voice for older adults' as a warmth and tone problem. It is a psychoacoustics plus telephony-bandwidth problem, and the fix is measurable in word-recognition scores, which makes it sellable. Older listeners can't tell they are the problem, so they just stop answering.
first_30_days: Recruit 30-40 adults 75+ from senior centers, paying $25 for a 40-minute listening test. Build a prototype on open-source TTS plus clear-speech DSP. Publish the intelligibility gain as a 2-page brief. Pitch 15 healthcare voice-agent startups with a free A/B test on 500 calls and aim to sign 2 paid pilots.

title: Idle Brewery Tanks as Biotech Pilot Plants
one_liner: Retrofit closing or underused craft breweries into shared 200 to 2,000 liter fermentation pilot plants for food-ingredient, cosmetic-ingredient and biomaterial startups.
customer: Pre-seed to Series A synthetic-biology and food-tech startups that need samples, regulatory batches and customer trials at pilot scale, plus struggling brewery owners who get rent or revenue share.
problem: Startups can make grams in the lab but face a valley before contract manufacturers will touch them: schedules booked, minimums high, and building their own plant is slow. Pilot-scale fermentation capacity is a widely reported gap. Meanwhile craft brewers are closing: 481 closures against 300 openings in 2025, and 9,344 breweries operating in June 2026, down 1.8% year over year.
solution: A 'bio-foundry co-op'. Lease off-hours tank time from 1 to 3 breweries. Add a portable sterile-air skid, in-place cleaning and sterilization protocols, a single-use inoculum train, and harvest and dewatering equipment (decanter or centrifuge, with drying done through mobile partners). Start with well-characterized yeast (Saccharomyces, Pichia) and other low-risk hosts. Sell fixed-price run packages, with brewer-trained operators supervised by a process scientist.
why_now: Breweries are stranded with stainless tanks, utilities, trade-waste permits and skilled operators, while beer volume keeps shrinking. Food and materials biotech has more strains than pilot capacity. The gap is at 500 to 2,000 liters, not 100,000, and that is exactly brewery scale.
revenue_model: Per-run fees ($8k to $25k), tech-transfer and process-development fees, a rent or revenue share to the brewery, and later a multi-year reserved-capacity subscription for repeat customers.
non_obvious_insight: The moat isn't the tank, it's the permitting: zoning, industrial wastewater discharge capacity for high-BOD effluent, food-grade utilities and a building already approved for fermentation take biotech companies years to secure. Breweries have all of it. Brewers are also the biggest pool of people who instinctively know how to keep yeast at scale contamination-free.
first_30_days: Sign a letter of intent with one distressed brewery on an off-hours share. Recruit 3 startups from synbio and food-tech directories and sell a paid $5k to $10k feasibility run at 200 liters. Prepare a biosafety plan and speak to the local wastewater authority early. Line up a part-time process scientist.

title: Exit Desk for Orphaned Local-Marketing Assets
one_liner: A fixed-price service that finds, takes back and migrates the domain, listing, phone numbers and ad accounts locked inside shrinking legacy marketing vendors.
customer: Home-service and retail owners paying $200-1,200 a month to Yellow Pages descendants, marketing agencies and template-site hosts.
problem: Thryv's 2025 revenue was $785M and falling, with net income near $0.3M, so the vendor base is melting through price hikes, resales and shutdowns. Owners often do not own their domain, Google Business Profile admin rights, call-tracking numbers or ad accounts, and leaving means losing the phone number painted on the truck. Getting customers is still the top small-business challenge.
solution: A fixed-fee audit finds recurring vendor debits (via bank feed or bookkeeper), checks who owns each asset (WHOIS, GBP owner list, ad-account admin, tracking numbers), then executes the takeback: domain transfer, GBP ownership transfer, number port, site migration into an owner-owned stack, and contract cancellation notices. Optional monitoring alerts if a vendor re-takes control.
why_now: Legacy vendor decline is visible in public financials, AI site builders make replacement stacks cheap, and small businesses still need customers.
revenue_model: $299-799 one-time, $29/month monitoring, and referral fees from the destination stack (hosting, CRM, review tools).
non_obvious_insight: What the owner is paying for is a person who answers the phone, not leads. The exit is a control and trust problem more than a marketing problem. The bookkeeper sees the debit but has no workflow to end it.
first_30_days: Partner with 10 bookkeepers to flag legacy-vendor debits. Run 20 audits and publish a 'who owns your phone number' checklist to seed leads.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.

title: Alpha-Gal-Safe Pharmacy With Verified Ingredient Sourcing
one_liner: A cash-pay pharmacy and lookup service that tells tick-allergy (alpha-gal) patients which pill in their cabinet is safe, by NDC and lot, and compounds the ones that are not.
customer: Adults with alpha-gal syndrome, who pay cash for a membership and for compounded fills. CDC estimates up to 450,000 people were affected in 2010-2022, concentrated in the Southeast, Midwest and mid-Atlantic and spreading. A second wave of buyers is allergy clinics, health-system pharmacies and hospital perioperative teams, who would pay a license fee for the database.
problem: Drug makers are not required to disclose whether gelatin, glycerin, magnesium stearate or heparin came from a mammal. The label says 'gelatin' and nothing more. The free Alpha-gal Information (AGI) mammalian byproducts database works at ingredient level, not for the exact NDC and lot in the patient's hand. A pharmacist verifying one drug spends 30-90 minutes calling manufacturers. Then the wholesaler switches generic suppliers, the excipients change silently, and a patient who has been stable for a year ends up with anaphylaxis or a 2 a.m. ER visit. Patients and their Facebook groups crowd-source this by hand.
solution: 1) Build an NDC-level sourcing ledger. A pharmacist team sends templated requests to manufacturers for written excipient-source statements, and an LLM parses the replies and DailyMed SPL excipient lists. Each NDC gets a tier (plant or synthetic confirmed, mammal-derived, unknown) plus the date and lot range. 2) Sell a 'Safe Fill' membership that dispenses only verified NDCs, pins the manufacturer with a do-not-substitute request to the prescriber, and alerts the member when a source changes. 3) Compound unavailable items into HPMC vegetable capsules. This fits the 503A 'significant clinical difference' allowance because a documented allergy is a patient-specific reason, unlike copy compounding. 4) License the ledger to health systems and allergy groups.
why_now: Alpha-gal is now recognized as far more common than clinicians assumed, and the lone star tick's range keeps expanding. Regulators and payers have turned hostile to copy compounding after the 2025 GLP-1 shortage ended, so the legitimate lane is narrow, patient-specific allergy compounding, and this idea sits squarely in it. LLMs make parsing messy manufacturer letters and SPL data feasible for a two-person team, which was not true three years ago.
revenue_model: About $14 a month per patient membership (lookups, sourcing letters, source-change alerts, substitution management). Dispensing and compounding margin on cash-pay fills ($25-60 per compounded fill). B2B database license of $5k-25k a year per health system or allergy group. Optional paid sourcing-verification requests from hospitals for one-off drugs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a list of bad ingredients. It is provenance per NDC and lot, which changes silently when a wholesaler swaps a generic supplier, and only the dispensing pharmacist sees the swap happen. Whoever holds a dated, manufacturer-confirmed ledger owns the trust of a patient group that currently does all of this by hand and pays cash for certainty.
first_30_days: Pick the 50 most-prescribed oral drugs plus anticoagulant alternatives. Send NDC-specific inquiry letters to manufacturers and publish a free 'verified so far' list to build search traffic and credibility. Join the alpha-gal patient communities and offer 100 founding members $9 a month for life. A pharmacist owner with a compounding license fills the first cash orders locally. Get a review letter from two allergists. File nonresident pharmacy license applications in the top tick-prevalence states, such as TN, KY, MO, VA, NC and AR.

title: Hatchery-Specific Phage Cocktails on Subscription
one_liner: A monthly service that isolates each shrimp hatchery's own Vibrio strains and ships a custom bacteriophage cocktail to kill them, so hatcheries can stop using antibiotics.
customer: Shrimp hatcheries and nurseries in Vietnam, India, Ecuador and Indonesia, plus the exporters and feed companies that buy their post-larvae and need antibiotic-free supply.
problem: Vibrio outbreaks (AHPND/EMS) wipe out whole hatchery batches. Antibiotics are banned in export markets, but residues keep turning up: a 2025 analysis attributes 43% of shrimp export rejections by the EU, US and Japan to chloramphenicol and nitrofuran residues, and 19 Indian consignments were rejected in 2025-26. Post-larvae pass through fragmented hatcheries and aggregators, so nobody can trace or fix the source. Generic probiotics and disinfectants work unevenly.
solution: A lab-in-a-box subscription. We sample water and biofilm each month and sequence and culture the local Vibrio isolates. We screen them against a curated phage library and ship a hatchery-specific cocktail as a water or feed additive. The cocktail is refreshed as strains drift, and later we add AI-designed phages. Each shipment comes with a residue-free 'clean seed' data pack that exporters and buyers can audit. Selling it in the feed-additive or probiotic regulatory class, not as a drug, keeps approval fast in most shrimp-producing countries.
why_now: Antibiotic bans (India's March 2025 notification banning chloramphenicol and nitrofurans in food-producing animals) are colliding with continued export rejections. Generative phage design became real in September 2025, when the Arc Institute and Stanford, using the Evo genome models, produced 16 viable AI-designed phage genomes from 302 candidates, later published in Science. Nanopore sequencing is cheap enough to run near ponds. Buyers now demand antibiotic-free attestations.
revenue_model: Subscription of roughly $400-1,500 per month per hatchery, scaled by tank volume, plus per-batch emergency cocktails at a premium. Exporters or feed companies pay a per-lot attestation fee. Longer term, license the phage library and drift dataset to feed and biosecurity companies.
non_obvious_insight: A phage is host-specific and keeps evolving with its target, so it works badly as a mass-market molecule and well as a perishable, local, continuously updated service. Big pharma cannot profitably do bespoke, and that is the wedge. The moat is the living library of regional strains and the resistance-drift dataset, and the hatchery is the chokepoint of the whole seed supply chain, so clean seed pays off downstream.
first_30_days: Partner with one university phage lab in Vietnam, India or Ecuador. Offer 10 hatcheries free strain-isolation reports to build the initial library, and pitch each hatchery a $500-per-month paid pilot. Ask one export processor to sponsor 3 pilots to secure antibiotic-free seed for its supply chain.

title: Continuity Assurance for Emotional AI Products
one_liner: A regression-testing and escrow layer that lets companion, coaching and therapy-adjacent apps swap underlying models without users feeling the presence they know has died.
customer: Builders of AI companion, coaching, journaling and tutoring apps with 50k+ users, paying $2-10k a month, plus $15-40k per migration project.
problem: Trend chain: labs retire models every 6-12 months (OpenAI removed GPT-4o from ChatGPT on 13 Feb 2026 and the #Keep4o backlash followed), then every app on a rented model faces a forced swap, then nobody can measure whether the voice, memory use, warmth and boundaries survived. Drift toward more sycophancy is also a safety risk for vulnerable users.
solution: (1) Extract a 'persona fingerprint' (tone, boundaries, memory behavior) from historical transcripts. (2) A swap-regression suite of 300+ scenarios (comfort, boundary-setting, crisis, sycophancy, memory recall) with human-rater calibration. (3) A portable memory-and-persona bundle users can export. (4) Optional escrow of memory and configuration with a neutral custodian and a shutdown covenant.
why_now: #Keep4o proved model deprecation causes real grief. Deprecation cycles are accelerating across vendors. California SB 243 (effective Jan 2026) raises documentation duties on companion operators, and the Pew data show public distrust that punishes visible harms.
revenue_model: SaaS by monthly active users ($2-10k a month), migration projects ($15-40k), and escrow retainers (about $500 a month).
non_obvious_insight: Users do not mourn a model, they mourn a relationship state (memory plus idiolect) that the app owns and can port. The lab's model is a replaceable engine, and nobody sells the warmth-preserving transmission between engines.
first_30_days: Interview 15 companion and coaching founders. Build a v0 eval on three open-weight model pairs. Offer free 'swap audits' to three apps, then convert the two most nervous ones to paid.

title: Licensing Workbench for Smallsat Operators
one_liner: A structured software system of record for satellite licensing across spectrum, debris, remote sensing and export control.
customer: Smallsat startups, university missions and new sovereign programs that currently pay law firms and consultants $50-300k per licensing cycle.
problem: Launches and deployments are at record levels (4,517 satellites in 2025), and licensing throughput is the hidden bottleneck. Operators juggle FCC, ITU, NOAA remote-sensing, debris-mitigation and export-control filings. Rules are changing (reported FCC rewrite, the 5-year deorbit rule, the proposed EU Space Act).
solution: A workbench with deterministic calculators (debris assessment, collision probability), templated filings, an ITU coordination tracker, deadline management and an insurer-ready data pack. Add a marketplace to hire specialist counsel. It is not a thin AI wrapper: the value is the structured filing data model and up-to-date rules.
why_now: The 2025-26 regulatory changes and a growing flood of new operators. The EU Space Act, FCC modernization and stricter debris rules all raise the compliance load.
revenue_model: $1-3k per month per mission. Per-filing fees. Referral fees from counsel and consultants.
non_obvious_insight: Every launch boom makes regulatory throughput the binding constraint. The company that owns the data model of a filing becomes the system of record.
first_30_days: Interview 15 smallsat licensing leads about their last filing. Build one calculator plus a deadline tracker for a specific filing, for example an FCC debris assessment. Sign five paying pilots at $500-1,000 per month.

title: Verified-Outreach Ledger for Government and Utilities
one_liner: A system where police, courts, tax offices and utilities log every outbound contact so residents can confirm in 20 seconds that they really called.
customer: County sheriffs and police departments, court clerks, county tax collectors, municipal utilities, and state benefits offices, buying through state cooperative contracts. Banks' fraud teams later.
problem: Law-enforcement impersonation drew about 61,000 complaints and $1.6B+ from Jan 2025 to Jul 2026, now with AI and fake video calls. The public message is 'the government never calls, hang up', which makes real outreach (jury duty, warrant notices, benefits recertification, shutoff notices) fail. Honest institutions can no longer reach people.
solution: Staff log each outreach in a lightweight tool or via CAD/CRM integration, and each contact gets a short code read aloud. Residents verify by calling or texting a verification number or visiting a page on the agency's .gov domain, which confirms agency, staffer, purpose and callback line. It also supports missed-contact reports and a library of 'we will never ask' scripts, and logs scam attempts for reporting.
why_now: The FBI's Sep 17 2026 PSA on law-enforcement impersonation makes the pain current, and video-call impersonation defeats 'just check the caller' advice. Google's on-device scam detection helps only one channel. Agencies have grant money for fraud outreach.
revenue_model: $3-12K per year per small agency via cooperative purchasing, $30-50K for a county-wide deployment, and per-message fees for banks and utilities.
non_obvious_insight: The second-order damage of the scam wave is trust deflation. Every warning that trains people to distrust callers makes legitimate callers less effective. The fix is to make the legitimate caller provable, not chase the fraudulent one.
first_30_days: Build a simple web tool plus a Twilio verification line in two weeks. Pilot with 3 sheriff's offices and one county court via a state sheriffs' association at $250 per month, and have them include codes on real warrant and jury notices.

title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

title: Half-Plate GLP-1 Menus for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A menu-engineering kit that converts an independent restaurant's existing dishes into protein-first half-plates priced at about 65-75% of the full plate, to capture GLP-1 households that eat out smaller but still eat out.
customer: Independent and regional restaurants (10-60 seats, $1-4M revenue) in metros with a high share of higher-income Gen X and Boomer diners, paying $499 setup plus $99-149/month.
problem: Circana estimates 23% of US households now include a GLP-1 user and that these users will account for about 35% of food and beverage sales by 2030. Those households cut traditional retail food and beverage purchases, especially high-carb, high-sugar, refrigerated and frozen items, and shift toward protein, fiber, fresh produce and restaurant spending, yet they still outspend non-users. Big chains are chasing this, but independents have no menu-engineering staff. If they simply shrink portions at the same price, GLP-1 customers feel ripped off. If they shrink and cut the price proportionally, margins collapse.
solution: For each restaurant, a done-for-you overlay: 4-6 existing dishes re-specified as half-plates with protein grams, plate-cost and margin tables, pricing at 65-75% of full price to protect gross margin per cover, a small-plate 'protein first' section, and a nausea-friendly option (low-fat, low-volume). Deliverables include a printable menu insert, a QR page, POS/online-ordering item entries (Toast, Square, Clover) and simple local marketing via medspas, GLP-1 telehealth clinics and pharmacies that hand out a 'restaurants near you that fit your plan' card. Protein numbers come from recipe-level calculations, not vague 'healthy' badges.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is at household scale (Circana, November 2025), and oral versions (Wegovy pill December 2025, Foundayo April 2026) plus cash prices as low as $149-$299/month on TrumpRx.gov are pulling in more users. Novo Nordisk is cutting list prices to $675/month in January 2027. Meanwhile restaurant spending is recovering, with independents beating national chains and Gen Z leading (BofA, August 2026), so independent owners are looking for a differentiator national brands cannot copy quickly.
revenue_model: $499 one-time setup, $99-149/month for menu updates, QR/landing page and local partnership marketing. Optional performance share (for example, $1 per redeemed 'plan card'). Later: bulk licensing to regional chains and food-service distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The obvious read is 'GLP-1 kills food demand'. The data says something different: users cut retail food but restaurant spending rises and total spend still exceeds non-users, so the demand shifts channel and portion size rather than disappearing. The winner is margin engineering (a half-plate that keeps dollars per cover), not a health-halo badge. Evidence: Circana (Nov 18, 2025) https://www.circana.com/post/glp-1-medication-users-to-represent-35-percent-of-u-s-food-and-beverage-sales-by-2030 and https://www.circana.com/insights-hub/glp-1s-consumer-behavior (23% of households, 35% by 2030, restaurants up, retail food down, users skew Gen X with income over $100K). Independents outperform chains: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/restaurants-and-discretionary-spending.html . Caveat: the Circana pages I could read did not give the size of the restaurant-spend lift, so validate it with a few owners' POS data.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Walk in on 20 independent restaurants with a one-page free audit of their own top 5 dishes (protein grams, half-plate cost and price). Convert 5-8 into paid setups. In parallel, sign 2-3 medspas or pharmacies to hand out the plan card and track redemptions to build a case study. Target: 5 paying restaurants and one measurable uplift story (covers or check average on half-plates) by day 30.

title: Landlord Loan Radar for Office Tenants
one_liner: Monitoring and lease-audit software that warns small office tenants when their landlord's loan is heading for trouble and recovers overbilled operating expenses.
customer: Tenants of 3,000-40,000 sf in office buildings (law, accounting, medical, nonprofit), their tenant-rep brokers, and office managers.
problem: With 17.8% national vacancy, 13.2% office CMBS delinquency and $39B maturing in a year, tenants sign renewals blind to the landlord's debt cliff. Distressed landlords may stop funding improvements or cut services, and operating-expense pass-throughs (gross-up, admin-fee caps, capital items) are often mis-billed, especially at low occupancy. Only large tenants can afford audit consultants.
solution: Public CMBS loan-level filings feed a radar that alerts on maturity dates, DSCR or occupancy drops and special-servicing transfers. An opex audit takes a lease and annual reconciliation and flags gross-up and base-year errors and non-recoverable capital costs. A 'renewal leverage brief' shows when the landlord needs an extension to refinance.
why_now: Elevated vacancy gives tenants leverage, distress is at a multi-year high, and document-reading software makes small-lease audits economical.
revenue_model: $149-299 per month per lease for monitoring, 25-30% success fee on recovered overbilling, and a white-label version for tenant-rep brokers.
non_obvious_insight: The landlord's refinancing deadline is public but nobody reads it, and a lease extension is exactly what a lender wants to see. A tenant who knows this can trade a signature for concessions.
first_30_days: Build a watchlist for three metros from public CMBS filings. Offer a free 'is your building on the list' checker and email 500 small firms in those buildings. Sell success-fee audits to the first five responders.

title: Rainbows End Book Scanning With Chain of Custody
one_liner: Vernor Vinge's destructive mass digitization of a library, run as a service where the AI customer is owner of record and gets clean text plus a custody certificate, never resold scans.
customer: Specialist and mid-tier model builders (legal, medical, engineering and regional-language models) and enterprises training internal models. The buyer is the head of data or general counsel.
problem: After the Bartz v. Anthropic ruling (fair use for buying and scanning print books) and the $1.5 billion settlement over pirated copies, buy-and-scan is the defensible path. But it takes procurement across thousands of sellers, cutters, production scanners, QA and custody records. Only frontier labs have that muscle (the Project Panama disclosures in 2026 showed how large it was).
solution: Acquire books on the customer's behalf under a bill of sale so the customer is owner of record. Scan under work-for-hire, deliver OCR text and a chain-of-custody ledger (ISBN, invoice, copy serial number, cut and pulp certificate), and retain no digital copies. Focus on niches frontier labs skip: out-of-print trade and technical manuals, legal treatises, closing corporate and law-firm libraries, university deaccessions and regional-language books. A rare-edition triage rule sends scarce books to libraries or an archive instead of the cutter.
why_now: The Project Panama disclosures, the 2025 settlement and public backlash over 'book burning' have made provenance a line item for legal teams. Specialist labs want clean data but lack ops. Production scanners and hydraulic cutters are cheap and off the shelf.
revenue_model: Per-book fee (about $1.50-3), acquisition cost pass-through plus 10-20% procurement margin, typically $25-100k per project, plus a premium for custody-certificate audits.
non_obvious_insight: The Bartz reasoning covers a lab scanning books it owns for its own training, not reselling the scans. The whole business must therefore be structured as an agent working for the owner, not as a data vendor. The scarce input is not scanning but acquiring legally owned physical copies of niche material at scale, and the certificate is what counsel actually buys.
first_30_days: Spend about $25k on a hydraulic cutter and two production scanners. Buy about 10,000 books from library Friends sales and estate lots in one domain (for example legal treatises). Run a 5,000-book pilot for a legal-AI or medical-AI startup, using a custody-certificate template reviewed by copyright counsel.

title: Robot Pack-Opening with Chain-of-Custody
one_liner: A neutral facility and machine that opens sealed trading-card packs on camera without human hands, sorts hits and ships them, so buyers can trust a break.
customer: Live-stream breakers and repack sellers, game stores running mail-in breaks, and buyers who pay for the 'bot-opened' badge.
problem: Fraud in streamed breaks includes resealed packs with hits removed, counterfeits and non-delivery. Whatnot did about $8B in 2025 and is under litigation, X-ray pack scanning is sold to collectors, and breakers spend heavy labor opening thousands of packs.
solution: A semi-automated cell (slitter, camera, card ID, sleeving) with serial-logged tamper-evident intake seals, a public feed with an audit trail, and a badge. Start as a neutral facility with humans in the loop, opening product breakers ship in, then lease the machine to large breakers.
why_now: Vision-language robot control matured in 2025-26. Litigation and fraud make trust monetizable, and the 2026 robbery wave favors a secured central facility over home streaming setups.
revenue_model: $0.40-1.00 per pack opened, per-hit shipping fees, badge subscriptions and machine leasing.
non_obvious_insight: Trust in breaks is a chain-of-custody problem, not a reputation problem. A machine has no motive to skim hits. Labor arbitrage pays for the machine while trust earns the price premium.
first_30_days: Rent a small secure space and run hands-off, sealed-bag-intake openings for 5 breakers with two part-timers and a phone rig. Charge per pack and prototype the cutter with an off-the-shelf arm.

title: Drone-Ready Rx Lockers as Adherence Infrastructure
one_liner: A lockable, temperature-buffered, authenticated receiving station at a senior's home that accepts drone or courier drops and quietly reports whether the medication was retrieved.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and pharmacy chains, paying per active station plus per delivery. Independent-living communities are the pilot channel.
problem: Drone delivery is scaling (Wing/Walmart 270+ sites by 2027, Lowe's launch on Sep 28, 2026), but a 78-year-old cannot reliably receive a 2.5 lb drop. Bending, theft, weather and controlled-substance rules get in the way. Plans lose Star Ratings money on medication non-adherence, and solo agers have no daily check-in.
solution: A roughly $120 bill-of-materials box (porch, balcony or window mounted) with recipient authentication, insulation and a retrieval sensor. Start with human courier deliveries into the same locker, and add drone-network integration as it opens. A missed-retrieval alert goes to the pharmacy, then the family.
why_now: Retail drone networks are now big enough to need a receiving standard. Part D adherence measures are triple-weighted in Star Ratings. Medicare Advantage benefit cuts (OTC benefits from 9.6% to 2.4% of plans) push plans to look for outcome-linked spend.
revenue_model: $8-15 per month per station from plans or pharmacies, plus a per-retrieval fee to drone operators or pharmacies. Optional hardware financing.
non_obvious_insight: The delivery event is the cheapest, least creepy daily proof-of-life signal, and no camera or wearable is needed. The receiving end, not the flight, is the missing piece of senior drone delivery.
first_30_days: Build 20 units. Place them in two independent-living communities where the operator controls the landing zone. Sign an independent pharmacy chain for human-courier deliveries. Bring adherence and retrieval data to one MA plan's pharmacy team.

title: Trust-Fund Compliance for Family Vloggers
one_liner: A minutes-on-screen tracker and escrow tool that computes, sets aside and documents the trust share owed to kids who appear in monetized family channels.
customer: Family channel operators on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram earning $50k+ a year, influencer agencies and MCNs, and brands and payment processors that want a 'clean hands' certificate.
problem: Several states have passed laws on minors in monetized content: Illinois (2024) requires a trust share by on-screen time, Minnesota (2025) restricts under-14 content creation for pay, and California extended Coogan-style protections (details from memory). Parents compute set-asides by hand. Brands and platforms are exposed, and grown kids and documentaries are fueling backlash.
solution: The tool ingests channel data, uses vision models to measure each child's on-screen minutes per video, computes the state-specific set-aside, generates records and moves funds into a custodial trust, UTMA or custodial investment account. It also keeps consent and deletion logs and issues brand-facing compliance certificates.
why_now: The state laws took effect in 2024-25, public scrutiny of family-vlogging is at a high, and a new custodial-account channel (Trump Accounts, opened July 2026, per the brief) gives set-asides a natural home.
revenue_model: $99-499 a month per channel or about 1% of earnings, plus per-campaign brand compliance certificates.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyers are brands and platforms that need a clean-hands certificate, and creators who need to avoid legal exposure. It works like marketplace sales-tax automation, and the child is the beneficiary, not the customer.
first_30_days: Ship a free on-screen-minutes calculator. DM 100 family channels with 50k-2M subscribers. Sell a $299 compliance setup with an attorney-reviewed template. Approach 3 influencer agencies for a group deal.

title: Rescue Orphaned Steno Notes With Stroke-Level AI
one_liner: A translation service that turns retired or deceased reporters' unreadable steno files into certifiable transcripts for stalled appeals, using a neural stroke-to-text model in place of the missing personal dictionary.
customer: County and state court administrators, public defender and appellate defender offices, and state AG appellate divisions. Secondary customers are retiring reporters and their estates. The first buyer is an appellate defender office with transcript orders stuck because the reporter left, paying about $2.50-$4 per page with a $1,500 minimum.
problem: Steno notes are a personal code, not a shared language. Another reporter cannot read them without the writer's dictionary, which holds phonetic strokes plus thousands of private shortcuts called briefs. When a reporter retires, dies or moves away, their untranscribed notes are effectively dead. Appeals stall for months, and courts may have to redo hearings or accept an inadequate record. Retention rules (California is 10 years for criminal cases and 5 for most others) mean old notes are also being boxed up or destroyed as reporters retire. The average reporter is in their mid-50s, and the workforce has shrunk about 21% in a decade.
solution: Train a stroke-sequence model. Input is the raw stroke stream with timestamps. Output is English with punctuation and Q/A structure. Training data comes from open steno corpora and community theory dictionaries, synthetic strokes with randomized personal-brief variation, and consented archives from retired reporters. Where the reporter also ran a backup audio recording, fuse audio and strokes to resolve homophones. Sell three products. (1) Rescue: per-page conversion, human-scoped by a retired reporter who certifies the transcript as prepared from the original reporter's notes. (2) Archive escrow: retiring reporters pay a one-time fee or a small monthly fee to have notes and dictionary converted, indexed and held by a custodian that satisfies retention rules. (3) Later, a scoping copilot for active reporters, who spend 1-3 hours editing per hour of testimony.
why_now: The 2026 retirement wave is here, and NCRA-cited data puts the average member age around 56. The 5-10 year retention windows for notes written in 2016-2021 are closing now. California's 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) requires courts to give indigent litigants a verbatim record on request, which will create more appeals that need transcripts. Sequence models can now handle noisy phonetic-to-text conversion with context, and the open steno community (Plover) has published theory and dictionaries.
revenue_model: Per-page rescue fees, priced below the $4-6 ordinary transcript rate and paid by courts or appellate offices. Escrow and conversion packages for retirees (about $300-$800 one-time, or $25 per month). Annual contracts with court systems for backlog clearing. Later, a $99-$149 per month scoping copilot for active reporters, who already pay $3,000+ for CAT software.
non_obvious_insight: Only the writer can read steno notes. Court administrators do not track how many untranscribed notes sit with reporters about to retire. The stroke stream is also a cleaner input than audio, because a trained human already resolved the speaker, punctuation and homophones in real time. Almost nobody outside the profession knows the raw-notes problem exists.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 retired reporters through state association retiree lists. They donate or license old practice files and act as reviewers and certifiers. Build a baseline model on synthetic and open steno data, then test it blind on their files and record the accuracy. Cold-call 10 appellate defender and public defender offices with one question: do you have appeals stalled because the reporter is unavailable? Close 2-3 paid pilots at the $1,500 minimum.

title: Pallet Co-Op for Micro-Resellers
one_liner: A distributor for one-person resellers that buys store-closing truckloads, values them SKU by SKU, and splits them into size-matched $150 to $500 shares delivered to each member.
customer: Under-25 and hobbyist resellers (roughly 3 to 100 sales per week) who currently buy at retail or from other resellers. They pay a markup of 8% to 15% plus a $19 per month membership.
problem: Real wholesale margins are locked behind minimum order quantities and size-run mismatch. A liquidator lot has 240 pairs, but 60% are size 6 or size 13 that nobody wants to hold. Mystery pallets are priced as a percentage of MSRP, not by what a SKU actually resells for, so buyers overpay for junk and underbid the winners. Discord 'group buys' exist but run on trust and screenshots, and they collapse when someone ghosts on payment.
solution: We buy truckload and pallet lots from liquidators and closing retailers, run the manifest against resale comps to price every line, and slice it: each member gets a share of the SKUs and sizes they selected, with the top-value pairs allocated by lottery so nobody feels cheated. Deposits are collected before we buy, so we carry almost no inventory risk. A partnered 3PL or a garage-and-labels crew ships each member's slice within a week. Later: net-14 financing on shares and buy-back of unsold slow-moving sizes.
why_now: Retail contraction is producing a steady stream of liquidation lots in 2025-26: Foot Locker is being folded into Dick's with store consolidation, other mall and footwear chains are closing doors, and brands reset inventory after tariff and demand swings. Margins on hyped Nike pairs are thin, so only good buying keeps micro-resellers alive. Cheap vision models make manifest-to-comp valuation nearly free.
revenue_model: 8% to 15% markup on each share plus $19 per month membership. Later, interest on short-term inventory financing and fees for a 'sell-through insurance' tier.
non_obvious_insight: Capital is not what stops small resellers from wholesale. Break-bulk is. Nobody sells a truckload in 40 slices sorted by size. The person who does the boring sorting, allocating and shipping becomes the small reseller's Costco. Because valuation uses resale comps rather than MSRP percent, the co-op can quietly outbid mystery-pallet buyers on the best lots.
first_30_days: Find one liquidator willing to sell a 5 to 10 pallet lot of mixed sneakers and apparel. Pre-sell 40 slots at $250 each in a Discord with deposits before buying anything, using the manifest value as the pitch. Rent a garage or use a local prep center. Ship in 10 days, collect testimonials and reviews, then run the next lot every week.
